questions.q: A bakery owns an unused oven and can add a second production shift quickly. Other things equal, its short-run supply is likely to be:
options: More elastic because output can expand without major new investment
More inelastic because unused capacity prevents adjustment
Perfectly inelastic because the bakery has fixed equipment
Unit elastic because capacity and price are unrelated
questions.feedback: Unused capacity makes it easier to raise output when price rises.

questions.q: Which situation generally makes supply more price elastic?
options: Production requires a fixed harvest already in the ground
All firms are operating at absolute capacity
The good must be supplied at one fixed quantity
Inputs can be moved easily into the industry
questions.feedback: Mobile inputs let producers expand or contract output more readily.

questions.q: A fresh strawberry farmer has only today to respond to a sudden price increase. Compared with supply over several growing seasons, today’s supply is usually:
options: Perfectly elastic
Exactly unit elastic
Less elastic
More elastic
questions.feedback: The very short run gives the farmer little time to change acreage, plants, or harvest capacity.

questions.q: A seller can store a product cheaply and release inventory when price rises. Cheap storage generally makes supply:
options: Unrelated to price
More elastic
Less elastic
Perfectly inelastic
questions.feedback: Inventory can be shifted toward periods with higher prices, increasing quantity responsiveness.

questions.q: Firm A can add workers and rent extra machines within a month. Firm B needs two years to build a new plant. For the same one-month price increase, whose supply should be more elastic?
options: Firm A’s, because it can adjust capacity sooner
Firm B’s, because long construction times create flexibility
Both equally, because price changes determine elasticity by themselves
Neither, because supply elasticity applies only to agriculture
questions.feedback: Faster capacity adjustment makes quantity supplied more responsive in the relevant time period.

questions.q: A concert venue has 20,000 fixed seats for tonight but can schedule additional shows next month. Supply of seats is likely to be:
options: More elastic tonight than next month
Equally elastic in both periods
Perfectly elastic tonight and perfectly inelastic next month
More inelastic tonight than next month
questions.feedback: Tonight’s capacity is fixed, while a longer horizon permits additional performances.

questions.q: Two firms face the same price increase. One has idle machinery; the other is already using every machine around the clock. Which response is most likely?
options: Both must have the same percentage increase in output
Neither can change output because price does not affect supply
The firm with idle machinery has the larger percentage increase in output
The capacity-constrained firm has the larger percentage increase in output
questions.feedback: Unused capacity makes output easier to expand, increasing supply elasticity.

questions.q: Suppose lumber producers can quickly redirect logs among several mills, while a specialized chemical plant requires dedicated equipment. Other things equal, supply should be:
options: Perfectly inelastic in both industries in every time period
More elastic for lumber because inputs are easier to reallocate
More elastic for the chemical because specialized equipment raises flexibility
Equally elastic because both industries sell physical goods
questions.feedback: Ease of reallocating inputs is a major determinant of supply responsiveness.

questions.q: A 10% increase in price causes quantity supplied to rise by only 3%. What does that imply about supply?
options: Supply is inelastic over the measured range
Supply is elastic over the measured range
Supply is unit elastic over the measured range
Supply is perfectly elastic over the measured range
questions.feedback: A percentage quantity response smaller than the percentage price change gives PES below one.

questions.q: Household income rises and demand for bus rides falls. This pattern is most consistent with bus rides being:
options: A normal good with positive income elasticity
A luxury with income elasticity above one
A substitute good identified by cross-price elasticity
An inferior good for these consumers
questions.feedback: Demand moving opposite income implies negative income elasticity and an inferior good.

questions.q: Demand for restaurant meals rises when consumer income rises. The income elasticity of demand is therefore most likely:
options: Exactly zero by definition
A measure of supply responsiveness
Positive
Negative
questions.feedback: Normal goods have positive income elasticity because demand moves with income.

questions.q: If demand for a good changes very little when income changes, the good has income elasticity that is:
options: The same as its price elasticity
Close to zero
Necessarily greater than one
Necessarily negative
questions.feedback: A small percentage demand response relative to income means an income elasticity near zero.

questions.q: A good has income elasticity of 0.35. Which description fits best?
options: A normal necessity whose demand rises less than proportionally with income
An inferior good whose demand falls as income rises
A luxury whose demand rises more than proportionally with income
A substitute whose demand responds to another good’s price
questions.feedback: Positive income elasticity below one is commonly associated with necessities.

questions.q: Income rises 8% and quantity demanded for a service rises 12%. Without doing anything else, the service is best classified as:
options: An inferior good
A normal necessity with elasticity below one
A complement identified by cross-price elasticity
A normal luxury
questions.feedback: Demand rises more than proportionally with income, so income elasticity exceeds one.

questions.q: A retailer estimates income elasticity for its store brand at -0.6. During a strong income expansion, the retailer should expect demand for the store brand to:
options: Remain fixed because elasticity is negative
Move only if the store changes its own price
Fall, other things equal
Rise more than income
questions.feedback: Negative income elasticity indicates an inferior good, so higher income reduces demand.

questions.q: The price of butter rises and demand for margarine rises. Butter and margarine are most likely:
options: Unrelated because cross-price effects cannot shift demand
Substitutes
Complements
Inferior goods
questions.feedback: Demand for one good moving in the same direction as the other good’s price implies positive cross-price elasticity.

questions.q: The price of game consoles falls and demand for compatible games rises. Consoles and games are most likely:
options: Complements
Substitutes
Both inferior goods
Goods with zero cross-price elasticity
questions.feedback: Demand for games moves opposite the console price, indicating negative cross-price elasticity.

questions.q: If a change in the price of one good has almost no effect on demand for another, their cross-price elasticity is probably:
options: Strongly positive
Strongly negative
Always equal to one
Near zero
questions.feedback: Little demand response to the other good’s price implies little economic relationship between the goods.

questions.q: Cross-price elasticity between streaming service A and streaming service B is +1.3. What is the best interpretation?
options: They are unrelated because only the sign of price elasticity matters
They are inferior goods because the coefficient is positive
They are substitutes and demand for one is fairly responsive to the other’s price
They are complements because the coefficient is greater than one
questions.feedback: A positive cross-price elasticity signals substitutes; the magnitude indicates a meaningful response.

questions.q: Cross-price elasticity between printers and ink cartridges is -0.7. If printer prices rise, demand for ink cartridges should generally:
options: Become perfectly elastic
Fall
Rise
Stay unchanged by definition
questions.feedback: A negative cross-price elasticity indicates complements, so higher printer prices reduce demand for ink.

questions.q: The price of tea rises 5% and demand for coffee rises 2%. Which conclusion is best?
options: Coffee and tea are substitutes with a positive cross-price elasticity
Coffee and tea are complements with a negative cross-price elasticity
Coffee is inferior because its demand increased
Tea supply is elastic because coffee demand changed
questions.feedback: The demand response is in the same direction as the other good’s price change, so cross-price elasticity is positive.

questions.q: A seller cuts price and total revenue rises. Over that price range, demand is most likely:
options: Inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
Unrelated to price
Elastic
questions.feedback: When demand is elastic, the percentage quantity increase outweighs the percentage price decrease, raising total revenue.

questions.q: A seller cuts price and total revenue falls. Over that price range, demand is most likely:
options: Perfectly elastic
Necessarily unit elastic
Inelastic
Elastic
questions.feedback: With inelastic demand, quantity rises proportionally less than price falls, so total revenue declines.

questions.q: If a price change leaves total revenue approximately unchanged, demand over that range is closest to:
options: Income elastic
Unit elastic
Perfectly inelastic
Perfectly elastic
questions.feedback: At unit elasticity, the percentage price and quantity effects approximately offset.

questions.q: A firm sells 200 units at $15 each. Which expression gives total revenue?
questions.feedback: Total revenue equals price multiplied by quantity sold.

questions.q: On a linear demand curve, total revenue is typically highest near the point where demand is:
options: Perfectly inelastic
Most inelastic possible
Defined only by income elasticity
Unit elastic
questions.feedback: For a standard linear demand curve, total revenue reaches its maximum around unit elasticity.

questions.q: A price increase raises total revenue. Which demand condition is consistent with that result?
options: Demand must be perfectly elastic
Demand must have positive income elasticity
Demand is inelastic over the relevant range
Demand is elastic over the relevant range
questions.feedback: With inelastic demand, the price effect dominates the smaller quantity decline.

questions.q: A firm raises price by about 6% and quantity demanded falls by about 3%. What should happen to total revenue, approximately?
options: It cannot be inferred from percentage changes
It should rise because demand is inelastic over this range
It should fall because demand is elastic over this range
It should stay exactly constant because quantity changed
questions.feedback: Quantity changes proportionally less than price, so the price effect dominates and total revenue rises.

questions.q: A theater lowers ticket price and observes both attendance and total revenue rise. Which inference is strongest?
options: Demand was elastic over the price range tested
Demand was inelastic over the price range tested
Demand was perfectly inelastic over the price range tested
Income elasticity must have been negative
questions.feedback: Revenue rising after a price cut means the quantity response was proportionally larger than the price decrease.

questions.q: A firm is currently operating on the elastic portion of its demand curve and wants to increase total revenue without shifting demand. Which move is most consistent with the total-revenue test?
options: Raise price
Hold quantity fixed by assumption
Raise fixed cost
Lower price
questions.feedback: On the elastic portion of demand, a price reduction raises total revenue because quantity responds more than proportionally.

questions.q: If demand is much less elastic than supply, buyers usually bear:
options: None of the tax burden
Exactly half of every tax by rule
More of a per-unit tax burden
Less of a per-unit tax burden
questions.feedback: The less elastic side of the market changes quantity less and bears more of the tax burden.

questions.q: If supply is much less elastic than demand, sellers usually bear:
options: Only the administrative cost of the tax
More of a per-unit tax burden
Less of a per-unit tax burden
None of the tax burden
questions.feedback: The less elastic side has fewer alternatives and bears more of the tax burden.

questions.q: A business facing highly elastic demand should be especially cautious about:
options: Raising price
Expanding output
Tracking competitors
Estimating variable cost
questions.feedback: With elastic demand, a price increase can cause a proportionally larger loss of quantity demanded.

questions.q: A business facing very inelastic demand can raise price with a relatively small percentage decline in:
options: Fixed cost
Supply elasticity
Producer technology
Quantity demanded
questions.feedback: Inelastic demand means quantity demanded responds proportionally less than price.

questions.q: Other things equal, a tax creates larger quantity distortions when demand and supply are:
options: Perfectly vertical
Unrelated to price
More elastic
More inelastic
questions.feedback: More responsive buyers and sellers reduce traded quantity more when a tax wedge is introduced.

questions.q: A policy that raises price will reduce consumption most strongly when demand is:
options: Independent of price
More elastic
More inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
questions.feedback: Elastic demand produces a larger percentage quantity response to a given percentage price change.

questions.q: An export industry can expand output more after a world-price increase when its supply is:
options: More elastic
More inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
Measured only by income elasticity
questions.feedback: More elastic supply allows producers to respond more strongly to the higher price.

questions.q: If employers can easily substitute machines for a type of labor when wages rise, demand for that labor is likely to be:
options: More inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
Unrelated to substitution possibilities
More elastic
questions.feedback: Availability of substitutes makes factor demand more responsive to its price.

questions.q: A city wants a fee to sharply reduce use of a service. The fee is more likely to change behavior when demand for the service is:
options: Perfectly inelastic
Vertical at every price
Elastic
Inelastic
questions.feedback: Elastic demand means usage responds strongly to a price-like charge.

questions.q: Demand elasticity is 0.3 and supply elasticity is 1.4. Which side is likely to bear more of a new per-unit tax?
options: The government, because elasticities determine revenue only
Buyers, because demand is less elastic
Sellers, because supply is more elastic
Both exactly equally
questions.feedback: The demand side is less responsive and therefore bears more of the tax burden.

questions.q: A firm estimates demand elasticity at 2.1. If its only goal is to raise total revenue and demand does not shift, which price move is more promising?
options: A price decrease
A price increase
No price can affect revenue
A higher fixed cost
questions.feedback: Elastic demand means a price cut can raise total revenue through a more-than-proportional quantity increase.

questions.q: Two markets face the same tax. Market A has very elastic demand and supply; Market B has very inelastic demand and supply. Which market should experience the larger reduction in quantity traded?
options: Market B
Both must have the same quantity change
Neither market changes quantity under a tax
Market A
questions.feedback: More elastic buyers and sellers respond more strongly to the tax-created price wedge.

questions.q: A conservation surcharge is intended to reduce water use. Which condition makes the surcharge least effective at changing quantity demanded in the short run?
options: Many close substitutes for water use
A long adjustment horizon
Very inelastic water demand
Very elastic water demand
questions.feedback: When demand is very inelastic, quantity responds little to the higher effective price.

questions.q: A tax is imposed in a market with very inelastic demand and very elastic supply. Which combination is most likely?
options: Consumers bear little of the tax and quantity rises
Consumers bear most of the tax and quantity falls relatively little
Producers bear most of the tax and quantity falls sharply
The burden is split equally and quantity cannot change
questions.feedback: The less elastic demand side bears more burden, while limited quantity responsiveness restrains the decline in trade.

questions.q: A regulator compares two identical per-unit fees. In Market X both curves are steep; in Market Y both are relatively flat. Which claim is best?
options: Market Y is likely to have the larger quantity reduction and larger efficiency loss
Market X is likely to have the larger quantity reduction and larger efficiency loss
Both markets must have identical quantity reductions because the fee is identical
Elasticity affects tax incidence but never deadweight loss
questions.feedback: Flatter, more elastic curves generate stronger behavioral responses and typically more lost trades.

questions.q: A firm sells a product with few substitutes today, but several close substitutes will enter next year. Holding other factors constant, what should happen to the firm’s pricing power over time?
options: It should strengthen as demand becomes more inelastic
It should be unchanged because substitutes do not affect elasticity
It should disappear only if supply becomes perfectly elastic
It should weaken as demand becomes more elastic
questions.feedback: More close substitutes make customers more responsive to the firm’s price.

questions.q: A subsidy lowers the effective price of a product. Policymakers want a large increase in quantity consumed rather than mainly a transfer to existing buyers. Which market is the better candidate?
options: A market with perfectly vertical demand
Elasticity is irrelevant to quantity response
A market with more elastic demand
A market with more inelastic demand
questions.feedback: More elastic demand produces a larger quantity response to the lower effective price.

questions.q: Jordan is willing to pay $42 for a textbook and buys it for $31. What is Jordan’s consumer surplus?
questions.feedback: Consumer surplus is willingness to pay minus the price paid: $42 - $31 = $11.

questions.q: Three buyers value a pass at $30, $24, and $18. The market price is $22 and each buys at most one. What is total consumer surplus?
questions.feedback: The first two buyers purchase and receive surpluses of $8 and $2, totaling $10.

questions.q: A buyer would pay up to $75 for a repair but the market price is $68. If the buyer purchases, the $7 difference represents:
options: Total revenue
Deadweight loss
Consumer surplus
Producer surplus
questions.feedback: The value above the price actually paid is the buyer’s consumer surplus.

questions.q: A seller is willing to provide a service for at least $28 and receives a market price of $36. What is the seller’s producer surplus?
questions.feedback: Producer surplus is price received minus willingness to accept: $36 - $28 = $8.

questions.q: Three sellers have willingness to accept of $9, $14, and $21. The market price is $18 and each can sell one unit. What is total producer surplus?
questions.feedback: The first two sellers trade and earn $9 and $4 of producer surplus, totaling $13.

questions.q: A producer would supply a unit for at least $16 and receives $22. The $6 difference is:
options: Consumer surplus
Economic profit including every fixed cost
Deadweight loss
Producer surplus
questions.feedback: Producer surplus measures the price received above the seller’s willingness to accept for that unit.

questions.q: Total surplus measures the combined gains received by:
options: Sellers only
Government only
Buyers and sellers
Buyers only
questions.feedback: Total surplus is the sum of consumer and producer surplus.

questions.q: A market creates $40 of gains for buyers and $35 of gains for sellers. Which welfare measure combines both sets of gains?
options: Total revenue
Total surplus
Consumer surplus
Producer surplus
questions.feedback: Total surplus combines the gains received by buyers and sellers.

questions.q: A trade creates $12 of consumer surplus and $9 of producer surplus. The gain from that trade is:
questions.feedback: The total gain from exchange is the sum of the buyer’s and seller’s surplus.

questions.q: A voluntary trade is mutually beneficial when:
options: The seller’s willingness to accept exceeds the buyer’s willingness to pay
The market price is zero
Consumer surplus must equal producer surplus
The buyer’s willingness to pay is at least as high as the seller’s willingness to accept
questions.feedback: A trade can create gains when the buyer values the unit at least as much as the seller’s opportunity cost.

questions.q: If a transaction creates no consumer surplus but $6 of producer surplus, total surplus from that transaction is:
options: Cannot be positive unless both sides receive surplus
questions.feedback: Total surplus adds the gains of both sides; one side may receive all of the measured surplus.

questions.q: Which statement about total surplus is correct?
options: It ignores all gains from voluntary exchange
It can rise even if one side receives a smaller share of the gains
It rises only when consumer and producer surplus rise by identical amounts
It is the same thing as total revenue
questions.feedback: Efficiency concerns the size of total gains, not whether those gains are split evenly.

questions.q: If a mutually beneficial trade is prevented, the unrealized gain is best described as:
options: Lost total surplus
A transfer from buyer to seller
Higher total revenue
Producer surplus that still exists
questions.feedback: Preventing a beneficial trade destroys the buyer-seller gain that would otherwise be created.

questions.q: Consumer surplus falls by $8 while producer surplus rises by $8 and no trades are lost. Total surplus:
options: Falls by $16
Rises by $16
Must become zero
Does not change
questions.feedback: An equal transfer between buyers and sellers changes distribution but not the combined surplus.

questions.q: A market change raises consumer surplus by $18 and lowers producer surplus by $10. What happens to total surplus?
options: It is unchanged
It rises by $28
It rises by $8
It falls by $28
questions.feedback: The net change in total surplus is +$18 - $10 = +$8.

questions.q: A buyer values a unit at $70, a seller’s willingness to accept is $52, and they trade at $60. What is total surplus from the trade?
questions.feedback: Consumer surplus is $10 and producer surplus is $8; their sum equals the $18 gain from exchange.

questions.q: Two possible trades have WTP/WTA pairs of $50/$32 and $40/$38. If both trades occur, what is total gain from exchange?
questions.feedback: The gains are $18 and $2, totaling $20.

questions.q: A rule transfers $15 of surplus from consumers to producers but also prevents trades worth $6 in total gains. What is the net change in total surplus?
options: An increase of $9
An increase of $15
No change because transfers never matter
A decrease of $6
questions.feedback: The $15 transfer changes distribution only; the prevented trades destroy $6 of total surplus.

questions.q: In an efficient allocation, a unit should be produced when:
options: The market price is below zero
Consumer and producer surplus must be equal
The buyer’s willingness to pay is at least the seller’s willingness to accept
The seller’s willingness to accept exceeds every buyer’s willingness to pay
questions.feedback: Production creates a nonnegative gain when value to the buyer covers the seller’s opportunity cost.

questions.q: Efficiency requires goods to go to buyers who:
options: Always pay the highest possible price
Value them most highly as measured by willingness to pay
Have the lowest willingness to pay
Arrive first regardless of value
questions.feedback: Allocating units to higher-value buyers maximizes measured gains from consumption.

questions.q: Efficiency requires production by sellers who:
options: Can supply at the lowest opportunity cost
Have the highest willingness to accept
Charge the highest price
Receive the largest fixed subsidy
questions.feedback: Using lower-cost sellers preserves more surplus from each unit produced.

questions.q: Once the next seller’s willingness to accept exceeds the next buyer’s willingness to pay, producing one more unit would:
options: Increase total surplus
Leave total surplus unchanged by definition
Create consumer surplus with no cost
Reduce total surplus
questions.feedback: The next unit costs more to produce than the buyer values it, so it destroys surplus.

questions.q: The efficient quantity is the quantity that:
options: Maximizes consumer surplus only
Guarantees equal incomes
Maximizes total surplus
Maximizes producer surplus only
questions.feedback: Efficiency in this model is defined by maximizing the combined gains from exchange.

questions.q: If the next unit has willingness to pay of $26 and willingness to accept of $20, producing that unit would:
options: Have no effect on total surplus
Add $6 to total surplus
Reduce total surplus by $6
Transfer $46 from buyer to seller
questions.feedback: The gain from the unit is $26 - $20 = $6.

questions.q: Four buyers value a unit at $40, $32, $25, and $18. Four sellers have costs of $12, $20, $27, and $35. Pairing highest-value buyers with lowest-cost sellers, how many trades are efficient?
questions.feedback: The first two trades have WTP above cost; the third would have WTP $25 below cost $27.

questions.q: A market currently produces 6 units. The seventh unit has WTP $44 and WTA $39; the eighth has WTP $36 and WTA $41. What is the efficient quantity?
options: 6 units
8 units
The quantity cannot be determined from marginal values
7 units
questions.feedback: The seventh adds $5 of surplus, while the eighth would destroy $5.

questions.q: Two allocation plans produce the same number of units. Plan A gives the units to buyers with WTP $30 and $28; Plan B gives them to buyers with WTP $30 and $20. Production costs are identical. Which plan is more efficient?
options: Both are equally efficient because quantity is the same
Efficiency depends only on seller surplus
Plan A
Plan B
questions.feedback: With identical costs, allocating the second unit to the buyer with WTP $28 creates more total surplus.

questions.q: If a policy merely transfers $10 of surplus from buyers to sellers and no trades change, total surplus:
options: Must equal zero
Is unchanged
Falls by $10
Rises by $10
questions.feedback: A pure transfer changes who receives surplus, not the combined amount.

questions.q: If a policy prevents mutually beneficial trades, total surplus generally:
options: Falls
Rises
Is guaranteed to stay constant
Becomes equal to government revenue
questions.feedback: Prevented beneficial exchanges eliminate gains that would otherwise exist.

questions.q: When market price rises and the same units continue to trade, consumer surplus generally:
options: Rises
Must stay constant
Becomes producer surplus one-for-one in every case
Falls
questions.feedback: Buyers pay more for the same units, reducing their value-minus-price gains.

questions.q: When market price rises and the same units continue to trade, producer surplus generally:
options: Must stay constant
Becomes consumer surplus
Rises
Falls
questions.feedback: Sellers receive a higher price relative to their willingness to accept.

questions.q: A policy causes some trades with positive gains to disappear. The value of those lost gains is:
options: Guaranteed government revenue
A loss in total surplus
A pure transfer between buyers and sellers
Additional consumer surplus
questions.feedback: Lost mutually beneficial trades reduce the combined gains available in the market.

questions.q: A policy transfers $22 of surplus from consumers to producers and, separately, prevents trades worth $9 in total gains. Compared with the original market, total surplus changes by:
questions.feedback: The $22 transfer changes distribution only; the separately lost trades reduce total surplus by $9.

questions.q: A price change transfers $30 from consumers to producers and also reduces mutually beneficial trades by $12. What is the efficiency effect?
options: Total surplus rises by $18
Total surplus falls by $42
Total surplus is unchanged
Total surplus falls by $12
questions.feedback: The $30 is a transfer; only the $12 of lost gains reduces total surplus.

questions.q: A rule lowers consumer surplus by $25 and raises producer surplus by $19. If there are no other gains or losses, what happened to total surplus?
options: It rose by $6
It was unchanged
It fell by $6
It rose by $44
questions.feedback: Add the changes: -$25 + $19 = -$6.

questions.q: A market outcome can maximize total surplus but still raise concerns about:
options: Whether buyers have preferences
Equity or distribution
Whether any exchange occurred
Whether prices exist
questions.feedback: Efficiency and equity are different criteria; maximizing total gains does not determine how those gains are shared.

questions.q: Why can willingness to pay understate the importance of a good to a low-income consumer?
options: Ability to pay can constrain the amount the consumer can bid
Willingness to pay never reflects preferences
Low-income consumers always have zero consumer surplus
Market prices automatically correct income differences
questions.feedback: Observed willingness to pay reflects both preferences and purchasing power.

questions.q: Surplus analysis by itself does not determine whether an outcome is:
options: Efficient in the total-surplus sense
Based on voluntary exchange
Associated with gains from trade
Fair
questions.feedback: Total surplus is an efficiency measure, not a complete theory of fairness.

questions.q: Two policies generate the same total surplus, but one gives nearly all gains to high-income buyers while the other spreads gains broadly. Surplus analysis alone can conclude that:
options: The second policy is necessarily more efficient because gains are spread broadly
Neither policy can be compared in any way
They are equally efficient by total surplus, but it cannot settle the equity comparison
The first policy is necessarily better because buyers have more income
questions.feedback: Equal total surplus means equal measured efficiency, while distribution requires an additional normative criterion.

questions.q: Suppose a market creates pollution costs not borne by buyers or sellers. Why can ordinary consumer-plus-producer surplus overstate social surplus?
options: It automatically subtracts taxes from surplus
It omits part of the external cost
It counts willingness to pay twice
It treats every seller as identical
questions.feedback: Private surplus measures can miss costs imposed on third parties.

questions.q: A rich buyer outbids a poor buyer for a scarce medicine even though the poor buyer’s health benefit would be larger. What limitation does this illustrate?
options: Willingness to pay depends partly on ability to pay
Total surplus can never be calculated
Producer surplus is always negative in health markets
Efficiency and scarcity are unrelated
questions.feedback: Dollar willingness to pay is constrained by income and may not measure all dimensions of social value.

questions.q: An economist reports that Policy A yields $500 of total surplus and Policy B yields $470. What can be concluded without additional value judgments?
options: Policy A is necessarily fairer
Policy B must have more consumer surplus
Policy A must make every person better off
Policy A has higher measured efficiency under the surplus criterion
questions.feedback: The total-surplus comparison speaks to measured efficiency, not fairness or individual gains.

questions.q: Market A has consumer surplus of $80 and producer surplus of $70, but production creates $40 of external damage. Market B has consumer surplus of $75 and producer surplus of $65 with no external damage. Which statement is strongest?
options: B is necessarily unfair because producer surplus is lower
External damage should be ignored because it is outside buyer and seller surplus
Private surplus favors A, but including the stated external damage gives B higher social surplus
A is necessarily socially efficient because its private surplus is larger
questions.feedback: A has $150 private surplus but $110 after the external cost; B has $140 and no stated external cost.

questions.q: Two allocations produce the same total surplus. Allocation X gives almost all gains to one household; Allocation Y distributes gains across many households. Which conclusion is economically defensible from surplus data alone?
options: The allocations cannot have equal total surplus if distributions differ
They are tied on measured efficiency, while choosing between distributions requires an equity judgment
X is more efficient because concentrated gains are larger per person
Y is more efficient because more people receive gains
questions.feedback: Total surplus measures the size of the pie; distribution of the pie is a separate criterion.

questions.q: A country’s no-trade equilibrium price is $18. The world price is $12 and the country is small relative to the world market. After opening to trade, the country will most likely:
options: Import the good because the world price is below its domestic no-trade price
Export the good because the world price is below its domestic no-trade price
Remain closed because a small country cannot trade
Neither import nor export because the two prices differ
questions.feedback: At the lower world price, domestic quantity demanded exceeds domestic quantity supplied, creating imports.

questions.q: A country’s autarky price is $9 and the world price is $14. In the small-country model, opening to trade makes the country:
options: An importer
Neither, because domestic price stays at $9
A price setter in the world market
An exporter
questions.feedback: The higher world price creates domestic excess supply, which is exported.

questions.q: Before trade, domestic equilibrium price is $25. A world price of $25 becomes available. Ignoring trade costs, what is the most likely immediate trade status?
options: Large exports because world price equals domestic price
The country must become an importer by definition
Little or no net trade because the prices coincide
Large imports because world price equals domestic price
questions.feedback: If the world price equals the no-trade equilibrium price, there is no price incentive generating excess demand or excess supply.

questions.q: A small country initially imports steel at a world price below its autarky price. Domestic demand then falls sharply while domestic supply is unchanged. What could happen if the shift is large enough?
options: The country cannot change trade status once it opens
The country could import less or even switch to exporting
The country must import more because world price is fixed
The world price must rise to the old autarky price
questions.feedback: At the fixed world price, a large demand decrease reduces excess demand and can create excess supply.

questions.q: A small country initially exports wheat because the world price exceeds its autarky price. A productivity improvement shifts domestic supply strongly right. Holding world price fixed, the most likely effect is:
options: Exports increase
Exports decrease because supply rose
The country becomes an importer automatically
World price falls because the small country controls it
questions.feedback: At the fixed world price, greater domestic supply increases the excess supply available for export.

questions.q: When an importing country opens to a lower world price, domestic buyers generally:
options: Lose because imports reduce choice
Are unaffected because only producers trade
Pay the old domestic price by definition
Gain because they pay a lower price
questions.feedback: The lower domestic price raises consumer surplus for buyers.

questions.q: When an importing country opens to trade at a lower price, domestic producers generally:
options: Are unaffected by the lower domestic price
Receive tariff revenue automatically
Lose some producer surplus
Gain producer surplus because imports raise price
questions.feedback: Domestic sellers receive a lower price and sell less, reducing producer surplus.

questions.q: When an exporting country opens to a higher world price, domestic producers generally:
options: Pay the world price to consumers
Gain producer surplus
Lose producer surplus
Are unaffected because exports go abroad
questions.feedback: The higher domestic price and larger domestic production raise producer surplus.

questions.q: The standard small-country model predicts that opening to free trade:
options: Raises total surplus even though some domestic groups can lose
Makes every domestic person better off
Always lowers consumer surplus
Always lowers producer surplus
questions.feedback: Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers.

questions.q: After an importing market opens, domestic consumers gain $90 of surplus while domestic producers lose $55. Which statement describes the national welfare effect in the standard model?
options: Total surplus falls by $145 because one group loses
Total surplus is unchanged because gains and losses offset by definition
Producer surplus rises by $35 because imports expand
Total surplus rises by $35 even though producers lose
questions.feedback: The consumer gain exceeds the producer loss by $35, so national total surplus rises while distribution shifts toward consumers.

questions.q: Opening an export market gives domestic producers $70 more surplus but costs domestic consumers $46 of surplus. What is the best summary?
options: There is no national gain because both groups must benefit
Consumers gain $24 because the world price is higher
The country has a $24 net gain while consumers lose
The country has a $116 net loss because consumers lose
questions.feedback: Producer gains exceed consumer losses by $24, illustrating how trade can raise total surplus without making every group better off.

questions.q: Why can free trade raise total surplus even when domestic producers in an importing industry lose?
options: Consumer surplus is always larger than producer surplus
Consumer gains can exceed producer losses
Producer losses are not counted in welfare analysis
Imports automatically create government revenue
questions.feedback: The efficiency result is based on the net change in combined surplus, not on every group winning.

questions.q: Why can free trade raise total surplus even when domestic consumers in an exporting industry lose?
options: Producer gains can exceed consumer losses
Consumer losses are ignored when goods are exported
Exports eliminate scarcity
The domestic price must fall under exports
questions.feedback: Higher export prices redistribute surplus toward producers while creating a positive net gain in the standard model.

questions.q: After trade opens, one group gains $120 and another loses $85. Which statement is best?
options: There is a $205 net gain because gains and losses are both positive numbers
There is no net gain because someone loses
The losing group’s loss should not be counted
There is a $35 net gain, but the distributional conflict is real
questions.feedback: Net welfare is the gain minus the loss, while distribution identifies who bears the loss.

questions.q: A policy analyst says “trade is beneficial, so nobody can be harmed by opening the market.” What is wrong with the statement?
options: Only exporters can gain from trade
Consumer and producer surplus never change with trade
Net gains do not imply every group gains
Trade can never raise total surplus
questions.feedback: The standard result is aggregate: winners can gain more than losers lose.

questions.q: In an importing market, which pair is most consistent with opening to free trade at a lower world price?
options: Both consumer and producer surplus must rise by the same amount
Consumer surplus rises; producer surplus falls
Consumer surplus falls; producer surplus rises
Both consumer and producer surplus must fall
questions.feedback: Lower prices benefit domestic buyers and hurt domestic sellers in an importing market.

questions.q: In an exporting market, which pair is most consistent with opening to free trade at a higher world price?
options: Consumer surplus falls; producer surplus rises
Consumer surplus rises; producer surplus falls
Both sides lose equally
Consumer surplus and producer surplus cannot change
questions.feedback: Higher domestic prices hurt buyers but benefit sellers in an exporting market.

questions.q: In a small importing country, a tariff usually causes domestic production of the protected good to:
options: Decrease
Remain fixed by definition
Fall to zero
Increase
questions.feedback: The tariff raises the domestic price, encouraging domestic producers to supply more.

questions.q: In a small importing country, a tariff usually causes domestic consumption of the protected good to:
options: Remain fixed by definition
Become equal to exports
Decrease
Increase
questions.feedback: The higher domestic price reduces quantity demanded.

questions.q: Government tariff revenue is generated by:
options: The tariff multiplied by domestic consumption whether imported or not
The tariff per imported unit multiplied by the quantity imported
The world price multiplied by domestic production
Consumer surplus multiplied by producer surplus
questions.feedback: Tariff revenue equals the tax rate per imported unit times the number of units still imported.

questions.q: A tariff raises the domestic price from $20 to $24. Domestic production rises while domestic consumption falls. What happens to imports?
options: They fall
They rise
They must stay unchanged
They become exports automatically
questions.feedback: Imports equal domestic consumption minus domestic production; both changes shrink that gap.

questions.q: A $3 tariff is collected on 40 imported units. How much tariff revenue does the government receive?
questions.feedback: Revenue is $3 × 40 = $120.

questions.q: Why does a small-country tariff reduce total surplus even though it creates government revenue?
options: Producer surplus always falls under a tariff
The world price rises by the full tariff
Some lost consumer surplus becomes deadweight loss rather than a transfer
Government revenue is never part of national surplus
questions.feedback: Part of the consumer loss is transferred to producers and government; the production and consumption distortions are net losses.

questions.q: A binding import quota directly limits:
options: Domestic supply at every price
The quantity that may be imported
The world price in every country
Domestic demand at every price
questions.feedback: A quota is a quantitative restriction on imports.

questions.q: When a binding quota raises the domestic price above the world price, domestic producers generally:
options: Gain producer surplus
Lose producer surplus
Receive no price effect
Become foreign producers
questions.feedback: The higher domestic price benefits domestic sellers.

questions.q: Quota rent is the value created by:
options: The gap between domestic demand and domestic supply at autarky only
Total consumer surplus before trade
Government tax revenue collected on all domestic production
The gap between the domestic price and world price on the units allowed to be imported
questions.feedback: Import licenses can carry value because permitted imports can be bought at the world price and sold at the higher domestic price.

questions.q: A quota allows 30 imported units. The domestic price is $18 and the world price is $14. What is total quota rent?
A tariff and quota produce the same domestic price and import quantity. What determines whether their national welfare effects are identical?
options: Whether producers earn any surplus
Who receives the quota rents
Whether domestic consumers exist
Whether the world price is positive
questions.feedback: A tariff creates government revenue; a quota can create equivalent rents that may go to domestic or foreign license holders.

questions.q: A binding quota is tightened. In the standard import model, which combination is most likely?
options: Domestic price rises and imports fall
Domestic price falls and imports rise
Domestic price and imports both remain fixed
Domestic price falls and exports rise
questions.feedback: A tighter quantity limit restricts import supply further and pushes the domestic price upward.

questions.q: A tariff and an import quota both reduce imports to 50 units and raise the domestic price by $4. Under the tariff, government collects the $4 per import. Under the quota, foreign firms receive all license rents. Which policy gives the importing country higher national surplus, other things equal?
options: The quota, because foreign rent payments raise domestic surplus
They are identical because price and quantity are identical
The quota, because quotas never create deadweight loss
The tariff, because its revenue stays in the importing country
questions.feedback: With identical distortions, the difference is who receives the $4 × 50 transfer; foreign capture of quota rent lowers national surplus.

questions.q: A quota is set at the current free-trade import quantity and is fully binding only if import demand later rises. Compared with a fixed tariff, what feature makes the quota potentially more restrictive after a demand increase?
options: The tariff fixes import quantity while the quota fixes price
A quota cannot affect price after it is set
The quota fixes import quantity while the domestic price can rise further
The quota automatically lowers the world price to zero
questions.feedback: A quantitative ceiling does not expand automatically when import demand rises, so the domestic price can adjust upward.

questions.q: A domestic industry argues for protection because foreign competition will reduce its employment. What is the main economic weakness in stopping the analysis there?
options: Tariffs never affect prices
It ignores consumer costs and jobs/resources created elsewhere
Employment can never fall in an import-competing industry
Foreign competition always raises domestic producer surplus
questions.feedback: A complete welfare analysis includes costs to consumers, resource reallocation, and economy-wide effects.

questions.q: A new domestic battery industry asks for five years of protection while firms learn a production process. Which finding would give the request the strongest economic case?
options: Documented learning-by-doing is expected to lower future costs enough to offset the temporary protection cost
The firms would earn higher profits whenever imports are restricted
Consumers prefer the domestic brand even at a higher price
The industry wants protection with no expiration date
questions.feedback: A defensible infant-industry case requires a credible temporary learning benefit large enough to justify the cost of protection.

questions.q: A national-security case for protecting a product is strongest when:
options: Domestic producers simply want higher profits
Imports come from any foreign country regardless of risk
The protected industry has falling employment
The product is genuinely critical and dependence creates a specific strategic vulnerability
questions.feedback: National-security arguments need a concrete strategic externality or vulnerability, not a generic dislike of imports.

questions.q: A proposed tariff would save 2,000 jobs in one industry but raise costs for downstream firms and millions of consumers. What is the best economic evaluation?
options: Reject the tariff because trade policy can never have distributional goals
Ignore downstream firms because only the protected industry matters
Compare the value of the protected jobs with consumer, downstream, retaliation, and efficiency costs rather than counting saved jobs alone
Approve the tariff because any job saved makes national welfare rise
questions.feedback: A defensible policy analysis counts economy-wide benefits and costs, not one visible group.

questions.q: An industry requests “temporary” protection but has received it for 25 years and has no measurable productivity improvement. What does this evidence do to the infant-industry argument?
options: It proves consumers receive the tariff revenue
It weakens it because the promised temporary learning benefit has not materialized
It strengthens it because longer protection proves the industry is important
It is irrelevant because infant-industry protection should be permanent
questions.feedback: Persistent protection without learning or an exit condition undermines the standard infant-industry rationale.

questions.q: A country imposes a tariff to reduce dependence on a strategic input, but domestic production cannot expand and allied suppliers are available. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The tariff may impose costs without meaningfully improving security, so targeted diversification may dominate
The tariff must improve security because imports always create vulnerability
Domestic production will necessarily rise enough to eliminate dependence
Consumer costs should be ignored in security policy
questions.feedback: The policy should be judged by whether it actually reduces the identified vulnerability relative to less costly alternatives.

questions.q: A tariff raises domestic producer surplus by $60 million, government revenue by $20 million, and lowers consumer surplus by $105 million. Ignoring other effects, what is the strongest conclusion?
options: National surplus rises by $185 million because all three figures should be added
National surplus rises by $25 million because producer gains exceed revenue
The tariff is efficient because government receives revenue
National surplus falls by $25 million even though protected producers gain
questions.feedback: The net change is +60 +20 -105 = -25 million; distributional gains do not erase the aggregate loss.

questions.q: A protection proposal benefits a small organized industry by $50 per person while costing a very large number of consumers $2 each. Why can the policy still attract strong political support?
options: Efficiency guarantees the concentrated group should win
Trade policy has no distributional consequences
Benefits are concentrated while costs are dispersed, creating stronger incentives for lobbying by beneficiaries
Consumers always favor tariffs because each cost is small
questions.feedback: Concentrated benefits can produce intense political organization even when dispersed total costs are large.
